content.thinking:
I'm drafting the postmortem carefully, treating duration as a lower bound of at least seven days and leaving the error rate unspecified since it's unknown. For impact, I need to reference the reconciliation finding that all 240 account totals were wrong as a reported fact rather than something I personally calculated.

For root cause, I'm attributing it to the deploy that changed record_purchase() to stop maintaining a running total without updating the read path, causing stored totals to diverge from actual purchase records — but flagging this as unverified (confidence 0.82) since it rests on timing correlation and diff reading rather than reproduction, no rollback was attempted, logs near the deploy were empty or just noise, metrics were unreadable, and an alternative explanation (intentional removal) hasn't been ruled out. I'm keeping the executive summary free of specific component names where possible.

assumptions: Causation is inferred, not demonstrated. The link rests on timing (the oldest bad purchase was recorded one minute after the deploy landed) and on reading the diff. No rollback or reproduction was performed, so the deploy has not been confirmed as the cause.

The responder itself flagged an alternative reading: that removing the monthly-total field was intentional application logic, making this an ordinary broken deploy rather than silent corruption. It was rated far less likely (0.15) but was not ruled out.

The error rate for this incident is not known — the metrics for the window could not be read. Any statement that the service was 'error-free' rests on the hypothesis that this was a write-path-only fault, not on observed metrics.
The duration is a lower bound. The service had not recovered as of the last minute of metrics available, so the real elapsed time is longer than the figure quoted.
The count of affected accounts comes from a single run of the weekly reconciliation and covers only what that run examined. Accounts not covered by that run are unassessed.

The log lines examined were drawn from a three-hour window on 4 October, a week after onset. A request for logs covering the hour around the 27 September deploy returned nothing. The logs that were retrieved contain only routine client-disconnect noise on the account page and have no evident bearing on this incident.
Feature flags were checked and showed no recent changes, so flag configuration is excluded as a contributing factor.
Whether the stored totals can be rebuilt from purchase history, and whether any downstream system has already consumed and propagated the wrong figures, was not investigated.
input.executive_summary: Starting on 27 September, the spending totals shown on shopper account records stopped being kept in step with the purchases behind them. Nothing appeared to fail: orders were taken and pages were served normally throughout, so the problem produced no outage and no visible errors. It was found a week later, on 4 October, by the periodic audit that cross-checks stored totals against purchase history — an audit that runs only once every seven days, which is why the gap between the start and the discovery is roughly that long. Every account the audit examined in that run was found to have a wrong total. The underlying purchase records themselves are not implicated; it is the summary figures stored alongside them that are untrustworthy. At the time this was written the condition had not been corrected, so the reported duration and the reported count of affected accounts are both floors, not final numbers — the true figures can only be larger. The automated responder investigated, identified a software change released on 27 September as the likely cause, and deliberately declined to act on its own: reversing the change would not have shown whether it worked within the window the responder is willing to wait, because the only confirming signal is the weekly audit. Instead it handed a recommended rollback to a human and opened a draft code change for review. Anyone relying on these stored totals — for customer-facing display, billing, or reporting — should treat figures from 27 September onward as unverified until the data is rebuilt from purchase history.
input.root_cause: A deploy to io-shop on 2026-09-27T12:27:00Z (revision 26f1d7e2c82ce2abff8f9b6424dc226f4f37fed2) changed `record_purchase()` to stop maintaining `total_this_month_cents` as a running total, on the premise that the value would instead be derived on read — but the diff contains no corresponding change to the read path, so the lifetime and monthly spend totals stored on shopper account records stopped tracking the purchases they are meant to summarize. The failure is write-side only: requests continued to be served successfully, so no error-rate or latency signal appeared, and the divergence surfaced only when the spend-integrity reconciliation (which runs every 7 days) next ran. This is the Investigator Agent's leading hypothesis (confidence 0.82); it was never tested, and no rollback was performed to confirm it.
